opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to the fact that the problem we're trying to solve doesn't really have a clean benchmark. When you're building something like Asimov, an agent that's supposed to deeply understand a codebase and the engineering organization around it, the thing you're optimizing for is "does this actually help an engineer get oriented and make good decisions in a messy, real-world system?" You can't fully capture that in an academic eval. Public benchmarks tend to be small, self-contained repos with well-specified tasks. Real organizations aren't like that. Knowledge is scattered across code, docs, Slack threads, tickets, and people's heads, and a lot of it is tacit.

So if research is off in a corner optimizing some proxy metric while product is building a wrapper on top, you end up with a system that looks great on paper and falls apart when it meets a real team. When we co-design them, the product becomes the source of truth for what the research should be working on. We see where the agent gets confused, where it retrieves the wrong context, where it's confidently wrong about how two services interact. Those failure modes become the research agenda, and they feed directly back into how we train and evaluate the models.

It's a lot like what we saw in our previous lives working on reinforcement learning systems. The breakthroughs came when the environment, the reward, and the model were designed together, not in isolation. For us, the product is the environment. Real usage tells you what "good" means. If you separate those things, you lose that signal, and for a problem as fuzzy as understanding an organization, that signal is everything.

There's also a speed element. When the same team owns the research and the product, the loop from "we noticed this problem with a customer" to "we have a model that handles it better" is really short. That iteration speed compounds, and I think it's one of the only real advantages you can have when you're working at the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response says research and product should be co-designed so real product failures shape the agent's research and evaluation.

r002.rationale: It mentions tacit knowledge and team context but does not say engineers teach team-specific terminology for use in future questions.

r003.rationale: It argues research and product should be designed together and that separating them loses important signal, rather than proceeding substantially independently.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't actually know what the right product is yet, and neither does anyone else. When you're building something like Asimov, where the goal is for an agent to genuinely understand how a large engineering organization works, you can't sit in a lab and derive that from first principles. The hard problems only reveal themselves when you're inside a real codebase with real history, real Slack threads, real design docs that contradict each other, and engineers who have a mental model of the system that's never been written down anywhere.

So if you separate research from product, you end up with a research team optimizing for benchmarks that don't capture any of that, and a product team shipping features on top of a model that doesn't have the underlying capability. Co-designing them forces a tight loop. Someone on the team deploys with a customer, sees that the agent confidently answers a question about why a service was architected a certain way and gets it wrong because the real reason lives in a pull request discussion from three years ago, and that becomes a research problem the next morning. That's how we figure out what signals actually matter for understanding an organization versus just understanding code.

The other piece is that the data you need to train on isn't something you can scrape. The way knowledge actually flows through an engineering org is messy and tacit. You only learn how to capture it, structure it, and get a model to reason over it by being embedded with teams and watching where the agent falls down. So the product is almost the instrument for the research. It's how we see the problem clearly enough to work on it.

r001.rationale: The response says research and product must be co-designed: product work reveals organization-specific understanding problems that become research problems, and the product exposes those problems.

r002.rationale: It mentions tacit knowledge and observing where the agent fails, but does not say engineers teach it team-specific terminology for interpreting future questions.

r003.rationale: The response argues for a tight research-product loop, rather than saying differentiated product design should proceed substantially independently of the models.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that understanding an engineering organization isn’t just understanding its code. It’s understanding why the code is the way it is, what people are trying to accomplish, and what constraints they’re operating under. A lot of that context isn’t captured in a repository. It comes out when you actually work with people.

So the product is part of how Asimov gets that understanding. What work do you give it? When does it ask a question? How does an engineer correct it? Those interactions give you context, and they also expose the research problems you need to solve—whether that’s remembering a decision or recognizing that you don’t have enough information to act.

If you develop the research and product separately, you can end up improving a model on tasks that don’t reflect what makes it useful inside an organization. Co-designing them lets you build that feedback loop: real engineering work informs the research, and better capabilities let the product take on more meaningful work.

r001.rationale: The response presents product interactions with engineers as a way to understand organizational context and research as a way to build the capabilities the product needs; it says real work informs research and better capabilities enable more useful product work.

r002.rationale: It discusses engineers correcting the system, but does not say they teach it team-specific terminology for interpreting that terminology in future questions.

r003.rationale: The response argues for co-designing research and product, and says developing them separately can lead to irrelevant model improvements.

sol-6.1.text:
Because understanding an engineering organization isn’t just a question of understanding the code. It’s understanding why the code looks the way it does, what people are trying to accomplish, and which constraints actually matter. A lot of that context is implicit, and you discover what you’re missing when you put a system in front of engineers and ask it to do useful work.

So research and product have to inform each other. The research gives you new capabilities, but the product gives you a feedback loop: Can the system find the right information? Can it connect information across the organization? Does it know when it needs to ask someone a question? Those experiences tell you what research problems you actually need to solve.

If you separate the two, you can build something that looks impressive on a benchmark but doesn’t have the context to be useful inside a real engineering team.

r001.rationale: The response says research provides capabilities while product feedback reveals what the system needs to understand and do for a real engineering team.

r002.rationale: It mentions asking engineers questions, but does not say engineers teach the system team-specific terminology for interpreting future questions.

r003.rationale: It argues that research and product must inform each other, rather than proceed substantially independently.
